utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Just let us make sure first that interpretation is being conveyed regularly. If there are problems, please let us know, as usual. I see representations are okay. And Defence teams, yes, again. The middle man is absent in the Beara team. The rest seems to be full. You would have noticed immediately that Judge Kwon is not with us today. A reason is that he is away with another Judge of this Tribunal on official business and he will be away for the entire week. So we will today, tomorrow, and Friday, we will be sitting as per this composition, Judge Kwon -- Judge Prost and myself in virtue of Rule 15 bis, and of course we have Judge Stole as Reserve Judge with us. That's the first piece of news I needed to communicate. Second one is this: I have a personal medical problem that I need to attend to with some urgency today. I need to go to hospital later on in the day so I would ask you to cooperate so that we stop the sitting at 1.00 so that I can leave. Which basically means that we will try to work out, Madam Registrar now will do that, we'll try and work out a sitting with one break only, if possible. Tomorrow, everything should be back to normal, as this is nothing serious or that you should worry about but you know how things are here in the Netherlands. If I miss this appointment now it will be another three months before I get another one and that's if I managed. So let's go into private session for a while. I need to discuss something with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Any preliminaries? I see none. Madam Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I notice that you are receiving interpretation in your own language of what I am saying in English. If at any time there are problems with interpretation, with the reception or -- either because it's not reaching you or because of the sound level, please draw our attention straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. My name is Carmel Agius, I am the Presiding Judge. To my right I have Judge Prost, who is one of the Trial Judges. To my left I have Judge Stole. Judge Prost is from Canada, I am from Malta, Judge Stole is from Norway. We are missing one Judge today he will be with us on Monday but hopefully your testimony will be over by then and he is Judge Kwon from South Korea. Very soon you will be starting your testimony here. Our rules require that before you start giving evidence you make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath in some jurisdictions, that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, nothing but the truth. Madam Usher, who is standing next to you is handing you the text of this solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn declaration with this Tribunal that your testimony will be the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, make yourself comfortable, please. So, within a minute or so, Ms. Soljan for the Prosecution will be -- will start putting a series of questions to you, which we call examination-in-chief. She will then be followed by members of the various Defence teams with cross-examination. It is important that you keep your answers to all questions, irrespective of where they are coming from, Prosecution or Defence, the shortest possible but also as precise as possible. Don't try to answer more than you are being asked. Just answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. Otherwise you will be here for days and days and days. Do I make myself cheer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The other thing is this: If at any time, sir, you are feeling tired or you need a break, you only have to say so and we will have a break, all right? Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break at 10.45, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. How are you?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Good morning. I am very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... questions and we'll carefully listen to your answers. Occasionally I may interrupt you in order to clarify points. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: What is your name, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Ahmo Hasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1937.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, municipality of Srebrenica. I lived in a village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Is that where you spent most of your life?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of my life. Occasionally I would leave to go for jobs, odd jobs, agricultural work.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, where were you living in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: In 1995, I was living in Srebrenica, in the town of Srebrenica, because we had been forced by the army or the forces to come down from the villages to the town, so I was living in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And what were the conditions of life for you and your family during that time?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult because the humanitarian aid came sometimes. Sometimes they would let them pass from Bratunac and sometimes they would stop them or they would keep a couple of trucks for themselves, keep what they wanted, and then leave the rest to go to Srebrenica. This happened in Bratunac. Life was very difficult, especially towards the end. There was a shortage of food. So people had to go to Zepa and get some food for there. They had a little bit more food there. They would bring it in on their backs. It took 11 hours of walking to go there, to bring back some food for your children.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, can you please tell us about what you did on 11 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: There was shelling on the 11th of July, for five days straight actually. They were falling at Srebrenica, around Srebrenica, so on the 11th of July we wanted to get to the UNPROFOR. The UNPROFOR was located close to Srebrenica. Their main headquarters were in Potocari so we were walking, running, crossing the streets, the shells were falling, and we saw that we had to leave Srebrenica. They left. They took the wounded and put them on UNPROFOR trucks, and the UNPROFOR transported them to the main headquarters at Potocari. I also went with them and all the people had gathered there. It was a very long column. It stretched from Srebrenica to Potocari, perhaps, and they were getting off the buses at the factories that were there, the factories were full of people who had arrived, men, women, children, and there were as many people outside in front of the factory as there were inside because not everyone could get inside the factory. There was over 30.000 people there. I was among them. I had no possibility to get inside so I was sleeping out in the open, and that's how it was. When we went down there, that first night, the people had assembled together and then the shells were falling around the people, all around the people, because they didn't want anybody to escape, I guess. They kept shelling. And that's how we spent the night there. We managed somehow and then the next day --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I wanted to ask you whether you took family members with you from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. My family was also there. My grandchildren, my children, my wife, grandmother, they were all there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with you?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I had four grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how about children?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: My children left through the forest, two of them. And none of them crossed, none of them managed to cross alive. I buried one of them last year, the doctors found him in a mass grave, and the other one I still haven't found any trace of yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And why did you want your family to leave Srebrenica and go to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The shells chased us out. That's why we wanted to go. If we hadn't left, we would have been killed there. The shells were killing everyone. They weren't looking to see if it was a child, a woman or a man. A shell would just kill indiscriminately. That's why we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Now, that first night, the night of 11 July, after you arrived in Potocari, where did you spend that night?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I spent that night out in the open. I had lost my family. They were amongst the people, so I lost them and I don't know if they were inside, but I spent the night out in the open and the shells were falling outside. When we passed that night, the next day a Serb came with a loudspeaker and he said, "People, don't be afraid." He said, "Our soldiers now are going to walk around amongst the people, just to check if anybody has any weapons or anything like that, just to go through, pass around through the people." And that's how it was. Then the soldiers came. A few of them, they were walking around amongst the people. I saw about eight dogs. They were German shepherds. I saw eight dogs walking with them. And that's how it went for as long as it was day. When night fell, you could hear screaming and moaning and the shouting began. They started to take out people one by one, and then when -- then at -- in a certain place, if somebody started screaming, then everybody around them would get on their feet and then after that, after about 15 minutes or so, you could hear moans, a little bit further away from the people, where they were hitting, beating, killing. You could see different sounds, and then they would be getting lower and lower and lower and then that would be it. Sometimes there would be a burst of fire and then you would hear nothing. You wouldn't hear any screams or voices. And that's what went on all night. For a while, we were lying down to go to sleep, but it's not as if the people really wanted to sleep. They just lay down out of fear. Some soldiers came by. There were about -- there were two by two walking around. They would take some sand or dust and throw it on the people who had covered their heads and then when they would raise their heads, they would look to see who it was and if it was a man they would bring him out. And if it was a man, it didn't matter what age that person was, they would lift him and take him away, away from the rest of the people and then you could hear the shouting, the screaming. That's what went on all night. At one point, two soldiers came along, they walked amongst us. One had a bloody hand all the way up to the elbow. It was completely covered with blood. And he was asking the women there if they had any water bottles so he could wash his hands. One of the women asked him, "What happened to you?" And he said, "I hurt myself." And she said, "Well, we don't have water. The river is close by so you can wash your hand there." There went on all night. Nobody was trying to stop it. The moaning, the screaming went on. It couldn't have been worse. I think that it was hell on earth. They say hell is in the other world, but actually there is a hell in this world too, and that night I spent in hell. And then that day, when it was Tuesday, the day Srebrenica fell, then Wednesday, we were also there. I survived. I could see them bringing in bread in a TAM truck and they were throwing the bread to the people. I managed to catch a loaf of bread. I gave it to my grandchildren to eat. And they were filming how this bread was being thrown and filming the people catching the bread. They wanted to show the world how humane they were. But when they were committing genocide they were not taping anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: You say they were filming. Who was the "they"?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The Serbs, Serbian army. I saw them filming. They had binoculars, they were tossing bread out from the truck, and the Serbian army, the Serbs, were filming that. They were filming all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Was there enough to eat for the people who were at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: It wasn't enough. The quantity was just to be filmed. It wasn't enough. 100 per cent sure it wasn't enough. It was a very small quantity, maybe 100, 200 loaves of bread.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So after your second night at Potocari, what did you do the next day, on July 13th?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: On the 11th and the fall of Srebrenica, the 12th, I was in Potocari. I described that. On the 13th, I went out from Potocari. There was a barricade, a check-point, that would let through 200 to 100 people at one go, so that to avoid crowds. Approximately 15 metres beyond there was another check-point where people were separated, men from women and children. They were led away to a house. We stayed at that house until it was filled with people. When it was filled with people, one person, Serbian soldier, came and said, "Do you have any felt-tip pen?" One person said, "I have one." The other one said, hurry up, hurry up before the other --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: German marks, not felt-tip pen. It sounds the same.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: So he gave him the German marks and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: When the house was filled with men, I was on the ground floor, some people were on the first floor. A bus came and we were told, "You can go." We had spent one hour there. I emerged from the house. There were two buses, waited outside. We boarded the buses and were driven to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir I'll stop you again.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Vuk Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. You said there were other men with you in that house. Do you know how many men there were?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: There was a room. I couldn't say but there were people upstairs as well. I was on the ground floor in that room. I don't know how many people could be crammed into this room, 40, 50, maybe, I don't know how many were upstairs. They brought two buses. We boarded those two buses and we were taken to the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the house in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, while you were in the house, did any Serb soldier ask you for your name?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Nobody asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: In the house, did any Serb soldier interview you?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, I wasn't. I haven't seen any other. I just heard that person seeking money, German marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Nobody said anything. They would just say that we are being separated, that we are going to be interrogated, and then we are going to be let go to reach Tuzla. This is the only thing they used to tell us, nothing else. They didn't interrogate us on any other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And you were starting to tell us about how you were taken to the school in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: We were taken to this school in Bratunac. At Bratunac we reached the service station. Then we took a left turn and reached the Vuk Karadzic school. When we were about to enter the school, we were forced to leave the bags with food in front of the school. I thought, well, I'll take my food when we come back, but when they took us into the school, they never let us out so those bags were left outside. That night, as far as I can remember, maybe one, maybe two nights we spent there, they would take people out and kill them outright, throughout the day, throughout the night, without respite. They were working in shifts, a single shift could not cope with that. It was a 24-hour process. There were people killed, moaning, screaming, outside. One policeman entered the school when we arrived there. A person was there, close to the door. The policeman started kicking him, and while he was kicking that person, another Serb brought a hose, a rubber hose, to him, handed it over, and said, "Use this." And he took the hose, hit him two or three times but found it wasn't very handy, and grabbed a rifle and started hitting that person. He was bloodstained. His face and shirt were bloodstained. That policeman, I believe he was a policeman, he wore a blue uniform. He had a white belt, and a pistol in a white holster. And that beaten person, the beaten man, remained among us, but after one hour, they came back to the door and pointed him out and said, "You, get out with us." Of course, he was hesitant, he knew his fate. They screamed at him, "Get up." And as -- he never came back. We could hear moaning and screaming. We stayed there. Later, they said, as far as I can tell, one day and two nights. And then we were told that we are going to proceed to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... questions about the Vuk Karadzic school. You mentioned that there was a policeman there. Do you know if it was a military or a civilian policeman?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Well, now, could be a military policeman, judging by his holsters and belt, but judging by the uniform, he looked like a civilian. So I couldn't tell. I was not familiar with the uniforms. White belt, I remember military police wearing white belts, but the uniform was blue, and blue as in the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you also see Serb soldiers in or around the school?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They would walk around. They would sometimes enter the room and take people out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many Serb soldiers there were?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. There were many of them because they had a headquarters there. Most probably there were many of them. They sent people out to catch our people who were trying to go through the woods and they had a detachment of soldiers to take care of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did. Their soldiers, camouflage uniforms, they looked like soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And for the roughly two nights that you say you spent at that school, can you give an estimate of how many Muslim men were in the school?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I can tell you, we were told you are going to Tuzla, we emerged from the school, boarded the buses. We were not permitted to look outside because a soldier or two would be standing next to the driver. They were making sure that we won't look outside so we were supposed to just look in the seat in front of us. At one point, I managed to sneak a peek and saw seven buses, Bratunac-bound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Soljan, sorry to interrupt you at this stage but I see that you are embarking on another phase in your examination-in-chief and I think there are still several matters that the witness testified about which are not exactly clear. And I'm trying to take them one by one. Perhaps you can ask him first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please ask me. Maybe I've skipped something but these are details, minor details. It's not as if I had a script in front of me and I was reading out off it. I may forget certain things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I fully understand, Mr. Hasic, and please be patient with us. We are just trying to make sure that your presence here would be made use of to the best possible. Perhaps you can ask him first whether he ever served in the JNA, what he did, and how familiar he was with ranks, insignia, et cetera. Then we can proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever serve in the Yugoslav National Army?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: 1960, I came back home from national service. During Tito's time, I served Tito.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And are you familiar with military insignia?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. With the former ranks, but with the modern ones, they are being changed, I'm not very familiar with. I was familiar with the former ranks in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could he describe the uniform of a military police in the army, in the JNA, during peace time, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in peacetime, they would wear the same uniform as the rest of the soldiers, they would have a white belt and a pistol in a white holster, and this is what distinguished them as military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the colour of the uniform itself would it be the same colour as that of an ordinary soldier or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, yes, it was the same uniform. I forgot certain things. I left the army in 1960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was the colour of the ordinary uniform of the Yugoslav army, JNA soldiers, drab olive or what colour was it? Was it a green olive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it used to be, while I did my national service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you've told us basically that one -- in peacetime one would distinguish a military police from an ordinary military officer or soldier from the white belt and white pistol holster; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This is how I understood that somebody was a military policeman. Officers had special uniforms. They had either stripes on their sleeves or stars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And would a military police officer have any insignia anywhere on his uniform that would also distinguish him as a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't really remember anything else, any other insignia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] White belt and white holster, and since this was a long time ago, maybe something else was there, but I forgot because I did my national service and finished it in 1960.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. Hasic. Now, I'll take you to civilian police now. What was a civilian policeman's uniform like in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was blue, civilian police was blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blue uniform. And do you remember the colour of the belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the belt was an ordinary one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if they carried a holster and a pistol, the colour of the holster would also be ordinary leather? Brown, black, white? What colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, usually similar to the colour of uniform, maybe blue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now I take you back to one answer you gave to a question that was put to you earlier on, and perhaps you can now explain a little bit as we go along. Madam Soljan asked you -- you mentioned there was a policeman there. Do you know if it was a military or a civilian policeman? And you said, you answered, "Well, now, could be a military policeman" -- one moment let me read it first and then I will ask you the questions. "Well, now, it could be a military policeman judging by his holster and belt but judging by his uniform he looked like a civilian so I couldn't tell. I was not familiar with the uniforms, white belt, I remember military police wearing white belts but the uniform was blue and blue is as in the civilian police." So I will just ask you a simple question. So do I understand you now to say that the person that you saw there in the Vuk Karadzic school had the uniform of a civilian policeman but the holster and belt of a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know now. I cannot get round to it myself, whether he was a military or a civilian policeman but he was a policeman, as long as he wore a gun and a white belt. I remember that well. I noticed it straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's a military police in your language? What are the words, the Serbo-Croat words, for military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Vojni policajac" or "vojna policija," military policeman, or military police if there are more of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And did you see those words anywhere, either in their full form or in an abbreviated form, VS, on the uniform of that policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see that. I wasn't looking for such. I was quite frightened. I really did not notice such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you for that information. Now I'm going to take you to another part of your testimony dealing with something completely different and perhaps you can then answer my question. You are referring to the first night when you arrived in Bratunac, when they took you in and didn't let you take your food with you. And then you said, "That night, as far as I can remember, maybe one, maybe two nights we spent there, they would take people out and kill them outright, throughout the day, throughout the night, without respite. They were working in shifts, single shift could not cope with. It was a 24-hour process. There were people killed, moaning, screaming outside." So let's take it bit by bit. How do you know that people were being killed? Did you see anyone being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see with my own eyes, but I would hear them moaning and screaming, then I would hear a burst of gunfire and then these people were never taken back to my room or other rooms, most probably they were killing them but I didn't see them with my own eyes. But it is a known fact this is 100 per cent sure. They found some graves in Potocari. They found two mass graves very recently, mass graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, please try to understand me that we need to know exactly what happened in Bratunac during those two nights. The fact that they found graves in Potocari and elsewhere does not necessarily mean that those people were indeed killed in Vuk Karadzic school on those two nights when you were there. So you need to be very precise in your testimony. I'm going to hand you back to Ms. Soljan. I think this part needs to be elaborated. We can't have testimony which just assumes and concludes that several people were killed and shifts -- in shifts and -- on a 24-hour basis, et cetera, because at that rate I would imagine that the whole population of Muslims in Vuk Karadzic school would have been exterminated according to the witness so you need to elaborate on this part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm saying because there is no allegation that there was mass killing in Vuk Karadzic school. There is an allegation of opportunistic killing in Karadzic and some other killings but not to the extent -- all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, I'm still asking you questions about your period of time in the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac. Can you give an estimate of how many Muslim men were taken out of your room that were not returned to your room?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I could tell you from my room, some six, seven people were taken out. From other rooms how many people were taken out, I cannot say, really. I wouldn't be in a position to say how big was the school and how many people were imprisoned there but screaming were constant, daytime, night-time. We could hear bursts of machine-gun fire that would suddenly cut the screams. Then sounds of screams would diminish and then stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Just from your room, how often were people coming -- how often were people taken out of your room?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Perhaps after about an hour, a couple of hours. It depends. Perhaps in an hour or a couple of hours or in three hours. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And who took these men out of your room?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The soldiers themselves, in camouflage uniforms, soldiers. They did whatever they wanted. There was nobody there to say, "Stop," to prevent that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of the men from your room later perhaps, in the buses?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No, no. I never saw them again. It was over. Those people who were there, I didn't see them any more. People that I knew, I didn't see any more. I buried my brother last year. They found him in Pilica. He was identified. That was a brother who was seven years older than myself. Another brother I buried this year, on the 11th of July. He was five years older than me. They were at that time almost 70, the older brother was almost 70, and I was almost 60. I had passed the age of 55. I was almost 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll ask awe few more questions about the conditions in the Vuk Karadzic school. While you were there, were you allowed to go to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: It was allowed but with escort. They would line up in the corridor, four or five of them, and then as people were passing by on their way to the toilet, as they walked by, they would be hit on the ribs with the rifle butt. This would happen a couple of times, if people wanted to go out and then later people didn't want to go out any more. They were afraid, so they would just urinate where they were. That's what they did. They didn't want to go out any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you see this happen, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see that, of course. I saw them urinating where they were or to urinate in a bag. The others would rush because they wanted to drink, meaning that there was a shortage of water as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So did the soldiers give you any water during those two days you were in the school?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did. Had they not given us water, more than half of the people would have perished. They did give water but it was insufficient and they didn't give any food.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, did anybody require medical treatment, of the men who were in that school?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Probably they did require medical treatment, but why would anyone want it when they were probably be taken out and killed? What use did they have then of -- to get medicines? There were such people but what was the point of treating them and then killing them? They didn't let anyone go. Did they let anyone go?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, the soldiers, the Serb soldiers did not give -- you did not see them give any medical aid or medical treatment to anybody during those two days?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, not at all. If they felt sorry for people, they wouldn't have done that. Why would they just give people medical treatment? They didn't give any food. They gave insufficient water. The food that the people had was confiscated from them. Why would they bother to provide medical treatment for these people? They were not interested in that. I was living in a village --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll try to help you finish your testimony as early as possible. Try to answer the questions that are put to you with a yes or a no as required without going into further detail. I mean, we all understand here. You don't need to explain certain things to us, but certain questions have to be asked and they need to be answered. If they can be answered with a yes or a no, please restrict yourself to a yes or a no, and you will be out of this place much earlier than you think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir you said you were placed on buses after being taken out of the school in Bratunac. Who all was placed on these buses?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers and drivers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Are you saying they alone were on the buses or they were the ones who placed the Muslim people from the school into these buses?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: They put the Muslims in the buses to transport them further. They said we were going to Tuzla. They gave us some bread, couple of slices each. That was all. And then when we set off, we could see we were going in a different direction. We were not going in the direction of Tuzla but in the direction of Zvornik, and then in Zvornik the buses crossed into Serbia, seven buses, so we went through Serbia. And maybe somewhere near Loznica, they crossed back into Bosnia again, over a bridge. At one point, when they were already close to Pilica, they stopped and they stopped for so long that one person lay down in the aisle, this Muslim, and these people started shouting, "lift him up" because then you cannot walk up and down the aisle and they left lifted him up and they were saying, he's dead. They were just thinking that he lay down, just like that, but he actually died and they said, "Just take him out and lay him on the side of the road." And that's what they did. They laid him down on the side of the road and he remained there and then there was a person who asked if he could go out to urinate and the Serb soldier allowed him to go out and he went out and then he started to run, and the Serb soldiers cut him down with a burst of gunfire. He knew that he would be caught like that, but he, I guess, preferred to be killed by a bullet than to be the subject of genocide, and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you see the man being killed?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did see that. How could I not have seen it when I was sitting in the bus? I was sitting close to him. I was sitting next to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you actually see him get killed?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see him. He wasn't killed there. He just died by himself. He died of fear. Perhaps he wasn't healthy. Maybe he would have needed some assistance, but nothing of that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please wait for translation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: You had mentioned that the -- a man had died and had been taken out of the bus. A man who had helped take him out from the bus asked to be able to allowed to urinate. He then tried to run away, started to run and was killed.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you see him be cut down with a burst of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I saw him. He was in the woods and there were two bursts, the gunfire. The first one did not get him but the second one cut him down and he fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, how long did you stay on these buses?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: We stayed there for about an hour, an hour and a half, and it was already getting dark. I don't know what they were waiting for, and it was dark for about half an hour or so, and then we went to Pilica. We were almost at Pilica, at the entrance to Pilica, and then when we entered we turned to the left to a school or a cultural hall, something like that, and then when it was already dark, we took the stairs to get in, and they forced us there to take all of our caps off, all of us had to take our caps off. Us elderly men we all wore caps. They were the French kind of caps, berets, we were all wearing berets, we took them off there and we entered the rooms and the same thing happened there. They immediately started taking people out, beating them. You could -- killing them. You could hear screaming and moaning. If somebody would get up and look through the window, if I did it or somebody else did it, there would be a burst of fire, gunfire. They were killing outside. You could hear screaming, shouting, moaning, from outside. This went on like this. And I think that if I can remember correctly, I was there for one night or two nights, possibly for two nights, I was there, and then at approximately on the 17th, people were already being taken out for execution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he just touched on what I was going to refer to now. If he could be precise as to the exact date when they arrived in Pilica, this particular spot in Pilica, if he remembers when they left Bratunac and when they arrived in Pilica, whether it was on the same day and in that case, what was the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And when did the events that he is describing happen?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, do you remember the date you arrived to Pilica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you roughly tell how many Muslim men were in this building in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: In the room where I was, the room was full. You couldn't move around. If a person stood up, they couldn't sit down later. There was no space. It was very tightly packed in the room where I was. In any case, the room was full. I didn't go into the other rooms and I don't know how many people there were. You weren't allowed to go out. You didn't dare. If you went out into the corridor, you were hit with the rifle butts. You didn't even dare to go to the bathroom. Many of them didn't dare go to the bathroom. They urinated where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you tell how big the room was you were being kept in?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps three and a half metres by five, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Okay. And could you roughly tell how old the Muslim men who were being kept in the room with you --

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: There were some elderly people there too. Up to the age of 80. That's for sure. 100 per cent. There were also children of 15, 16 years of age. They asked who was 15 or 16 and they said, "Come, line up here so that we can see you." And there were about 12 children like that ranging from 15 to 16 and they said, "We need people or kids like this for Abdic, Abdic is looking for people like that and they took them out. I don't know what they did with them. This is what happened in that room. As for the other rooms, how many of them there were, how many they could assemble, I don't know. Perhaps it was 100, 120 of them that they assembled from the other rooms. In any case, they were taken out and were never heard of again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that they asked who was 15 or 16 and said to come up and line up. Who -- who were the "they"? Who were the people who asked the question?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Serb soldiers who were guarding us and keeping us there and doing whatever they wanted with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Could you tell how many Serb soldiers were around or in the Pilica building, who were guarding the Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I can say that approximately there were about 10 who were there, and there were another 10 at the place where they were killing, where the executions were going on, so the 10 there, the 10 were up there, then there were two or one always on the buses who were escorting and I noticed at the school that there was a deaf and dumb person, and one of our men asked if there was anything to eat, and this other guy said, "We don't have anything to give you." And then after about half an hour or so he brought a loaf of bread and he was breaking off bite-sized pieces and giving them to the people and I think, if I can remember correctly, we spent about two nights there. The following day, after those two nights, it was said that those who wanted to go to Sarajevo and has the money can pay for the bus to go to Sarajevo, and one of them said, "I have 100 German marks and I'm going to pay for my friend, my colleague, my neighbour. We can pay for five of us." And that's how people left. As long as they had the money, they could go, allegedly to Sarajevo. After people ran out of money, then it was said, "You are going to Tuzla," so now it was possible to go even without money. It was possible to get on the bus without money. And then after that, they brought two sheets. They were long ones. And they said, "This has to be torn into strips" and we were going to be tied up and two men were tearing them, this sheet, up, and tying our hands behind our back. And people were leaving, the buses were going quickly, and returning quickly. I thought, well, I was going to get tied up as well. Very few people were left in that room and I placed my hands on my -- behind my back and that's how they tied me up. We were going out, and as we were going out, going down the stairs, and when we reached the ground floor, there was a man who was dead there. There was blood, a pool of blood all around him. He was lying at the bottom of the stairs. He was dead. We went outside. We were going towards the buses. There were two buses there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Stop there, Mr. Hasic. Mr. Lazarevic, I noticed you before. Something wrong with the transcript, I imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour is right. What I have noticed when the witness was giving his evidence regarding this event that he had with Serb soldier, it's on page 28 -- in a moment I will find, yes, well, basically what I heard the witness saying is that Serbian soldiers said, "We don't have enough food for ourselves and that's the reason why I cannot give you food." And if Ms. Soljan can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hasic, you've heard what Mr. Lazarevic has just stated. Is it correct that when the soldier --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that. That was true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's true that he said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed, then, with the rest of the examination-in-chief, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, when I came down from the first floor, and I said --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I'll just stop you and just take you back to a few more questions about what was happening in Pilica. During the time that you were there, you mentioned that there was also mistreatment, there were killings going on. Did you see any of those killings happen?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anything. All I heard was moaning and the screaming outside. This went on day and night, constantly. It was incessant. They were probably killing in shifts. This is 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Soljan, because earlier on when he also said more or less the same thing, let me find it- apart from screaming and moaning which he has repeated now, he also mentioned, at least that's what we have in the transcript, bursts of fire, gunfire. What I would like to know is whether the screaming and the gunfire -- and the moaning that he heard was at the same time he was hearing the fire, the gunfire, or whether it was -- whether it was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The screaming and the moaning was before, and then after the screaming, when you hear the burst of gunfire, then there is no more screaming. It's finished. It's quiet. That means that they were get -- being killed. If we were to look through the window or if we were a little bit noisier inside, then the burst of fire would be directed at us, so we didn't dare look out of the window. And that's why we didn't see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall how many times these bursts of -- or the shooting happened?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It happened many times. I cannot describe it. I didn't count it at the time, but I also heard several voices, moaning, at the same time, when four or five people were taken out at the same time, they were being dragged here and there. I would hear four or five voices, sometimes, and then there would be a burst of gunfire cutting them down and then everything would be quiet and then after a certain interval, more people would be taken out. This is how it happened. And I saw this dead person there when we were leaving the school. I saw the person, the body at the bottom of the stairs as we were going on -- as we were on our way to the buses. One of the buses, I remember very well, was a Sedmo Julac Sabac bus. It belonged to that company, the 7th July company from Sabac. I don't remember who the other bus belonged to. I just remember this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: How big were these buses? How many men fit inside?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Maybe about 50 or so. We got to the buses. There were about 10 soldiers escorting us to the buses and when we reached the buses I looked across a little bit. I saw four officers standing in the shade. These soldiers were swearing at us, telling us to move forward. They would hit somebody occasionally with a rifle butt. The others they didn't do anything. They were just watching and perhaps saying a few words amongst themselves, and then we entered the buses. When we got on to the buses, and we were tied up, we were told that we were going to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Soljan, we've come to a particular stage now in the -- covering the events in Pilica. Until this particular time, when now he is together with others being taken out of the school, to the buses, and from the time he left Bratunac, apart from soldiers that he's been continually referring to, did he ever see military police or any other members of the armed forces or armed personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see military policemen. I just saw the regular multi-coloured uniform that they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether they were wearing any berets?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, were they wearing any berets?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: We were wearing the French berets, black or blue ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any of the soldiers wore any berets and whether you could see any ranks, insignia or any identification as regards ranks amongst the soldiers that you saw there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not looking out for insignia. I just noticed their variegated uniforms. There were officers for sure there but I wasn't on the lookout for that. People were being killed. People were terrified. I was terrified whether I would survive or not. There were times that I was counting that -- reckoning that my life would last only seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, up to this point, since you left Bratunac, did any of the Serb military ask you for your name?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: They never asked me personally. They would take out individuals, ask them questions. Some of them returned. Some of them never returned after being led away. Maybe if they knew somebody personally they would ask them questions after taking them out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did any of the Serb soldiers register you with the ICRC at any time since you left Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Nobody registered me. There were people who were registered but never came. The wounded who would be registered but -- he would disappear there -- are no more.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Did you see people being registered anywhere from Bratunac to your arrival in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I did not see that. I believe that they did the registration at the headquarters somewhere, where the Dutch government or defence was located. They did some registration there. I heard about that. I never saw that. I -- there are some of my neighbours who were registered but who never came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You said that you were placed, that there were two buses in front of the Pilica building and that you were placed on one of these. Were any of the Serb soldiers on these buses?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: There would be one or two soldiers. There were escorts, they would sit next to the driver. We would be sitting on the seats and were not supposed to look outside the window, just straight ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Were these the same soldiers you had seen in the Pilica building before that?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The same soldiers. They would escort us to the bus, we would board the bus and then one or two would enter the bus with us and the rest would stay at the school building. The point where we came to, there was a group of soldiers who would wait for the buses to off-load and then would execute people.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you travel in those buses?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a short -- it was a short journey, two and a half kilometres approximately. We climbed a hill. We heard bursts of gunfire. When we reached the place where there was gunfire, the buses stopped and as soon as they stopped, the doors would open. Serbian soldiers gathered round the buses. Said -- and they were cursing our mothers and us, and Haris Silajdzic's mother as well. They said, "They don't want you. Get out of the bus." And then death -- you could see death in their eyes. Until that point, you feel you never knew what was going, because they would say one thing, do another, and they started -- people started emerging from the buses and after the buses were half empty, they would stop people from disembarking. I was still on the bus and was looking at what was going on. They took the people down a path in the field, there are dead people, bursts of gunfire would cut people down. People fell dead to the ground. When this was finished, they would come back. I emerged from the bus. There were cursing, "Fuck your mother and Alija and Haris." "They don't want you." "Get out of the bus." "Come here." And you reckon there are still a couple of seconds of life left. When everybody disembarked from the buses with their hands tied, including me, we formed a column and there were dead people in the column, there were dead people on the path, you could see them lying on the ground. They didn't even reach the execution site. They were killed in between. One Serb soldier, he was walking in front of me, he said to me, there were some eight of them, walking next to the column, he told me, "Give me some German marks." I told him, "I don't have any." And I was ready to be killed. He kicked me in the stomach. I doubled back and crouched, started screaming, screaming for help, and the Serb soldier who was walking behind me, he called to the first soldier, "Don't perpetrate genocide, be a soldier about it. Take a rifle if you want to kill anybody." I stood up, and started following the column, and the soldier who kicked me asked me, whether I want to convert to and register as Serbs to survive? There are only two people in the column who opted for that, but to no avail. Even those two who opted for this, one of our people from the column asked, "Give us water and then you may kill us." You see how thirsty we were, hungry and thirsty. But to no avail. If somebody felt sorry for us, they wouldn't be leading us to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: 100 metres --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Was there anything particular about this location, any prominent buildings or other objects that stood out in this location, as you recall?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Where we disembarked the buses, there was an apple tree. I noticed a garden, and a house in some distance, maybe two. I couldn't notice, I was too terrified. And there was a ditch leading away from the homes, those houses, and there was a glen 100 metres down the path, this is where they executed people. We were put in lines and people lay dead in lines. We reached the people who had been murdered and we passed through the ranks of the dead, through the lines of the dead, and they would be expanding these lines starting from the top. There was an incline where people were killed. I was somewhere in midline. When we reached that point, there was a command, "Turn around, turn your backs to us." We did so. And instead of fire, they commanded, "Lie down." But before somebody issued such a command, they would open fire. I fell immediately. The others fell down when fire was opened at them. When the bursts of fire died down, one of them asked, "Are there any survivors?" "I survived," said one person, and the other one said, "I survived. Kill me." So they -- that person would go from one survivor to another and fired a single bullet to the head. I thought about notifying them that I was alive. I was contemplating if I could free my hands, then I would -- if I could not free my hands, then I would yell that I was alive and they would kill me but I reckoned if I could free my hands then I would be able to survive and escape, and there I lay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... supposed to be reaching our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish this part of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Please continue, sir.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: So there were seven columns of people that they brought here. I was lying down. Rounds of ammunition hit all around me. Fortunately none of the bullets hit me. They would excavate earth. I was hit by soil, by stones, but lie down, one hit me in the elbow. Nothing else. Seven columns of people were then executed. I noticed that they were dead. There were very few people remaining in my room. Then they took a break to the house where the buses stopped. They would sit down in the shade. I tried to free my hands. Fortunately, I managed to free my hands, and then assumed the same position because I knew that they would be patrolling, and half an hour later, a patrol of five soldiers came. I could hear them speak. I could hear their steps and I would take a peek every now and then. And suddenly I heard, "one of them escaped," "another one escaped." I would hear gun bursts and people would escape. One remained there of the five. Two of them came back after a while and said, "What happened?" The one who left behind asked, "What happened?" And the answer was, "When one of them hid, and the other two are still looking for the other one. So one was killed the other one was still being chased." One of them said, "We committed genocide, the likes of a genocide in Jasenovac in 1941."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will have a break now and it will be a 30-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were just telling us about you lying on the ground after the execution. Could you tell us how you were finally able to get away from the spot, the execution site?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: When they left the place to retreat to the shade, somebody close to me was whispering the second line, I turned around and whispered is there anybody alive? Let's get away. We were trying to ascertain the time before night-time. It was some two hours before dusk. I was trying to see whether there was a forest close by to hide in. People were lying in lines. I knew that they would be bringing earth-moving machinery. They wouldn't -- it was clear to me, they wouldn't try to bury those people manually. So below the field, there was a ditch, the ditch that I mentioned close to the houses, close to the spot where the buses parked. There was some shrubbery, some 150 square metres of shrubbery and trees. I decided to head towards the scrub, the shrubbery. I tried to free my hands to be able to move better. When I freed my hands, I took a look. Two people were crawling into the shrubs, shrubbery. I jumped to my feet to crawl some distance. I was afraid there would be a patrol coming back. I jumped to my feet. I decided to risk it. I trod on dead people, on soil. I tried to avoid treading on dead people but I could not avoid it. And I was listening for a cry, "Look at him, he's running away." I knew that if I were -- was spotted, I would be dead. I crouched and travelled some 20 metres until I reached the bushes. Two other people were crawling and they ended in the same shrubbery. The four of them, and I was the fifth one, we lied. Everybody else was dead. Among -- 1.000, 1.500 people that were killed there, in my estimate. So we were concealed in the shrubbery. There was a patrol. They walked around the dead, making sure that nobody escaped. We were close by in the shrubbery. They did not check whether there were anybody -- any survivors in the shrubbery. We lay low until dusk. When darkness fell, they left, and we emerged to the other side from the shrubs. There were dead people in the field as well. I did not know that before. Those were the people who were taken away in the morning, who were presumably paying their way to Sarajevo. They were killed there, probably. There were five of us. We crossed that field until we reached a forest. There was some moonlight. When we reached the forest, I couldn't see anything. I was exhausted by that time, thirsty, hungry, terrified, and I was of an advanced age. The others were younger, ranging from 16 to 25, judging by their appearance. They went away. I was left there alone. I didn't know what to do, where to go. My progress was very slow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Some five minutes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: You mentioned these four other younger men who were with you. Do you know who they were, where they were from?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I asked one. He said that he was from the Jagonje village. I didn't ask him his name. And I don't know it. I asked them whether they reached their target but I couldn't find out. They did not, because I asked whether anybody from that village managed to escape. They told me no. Maybe two years ago, I heard that they were captured, they were led away to Zvornik, and Zvornik is a notorious place. So I continued alone. I reached an ambush because they -- around the place where they executed people, they would set up ambushes to catch those who managed to escape. There was one who managed to escape. I started to cross the road. A soldier cried out, "Who is it? Who is it?" I meant to escape but I reached a village with some civilians living so I could not enter the village. I tried to hide where I was. That patrol started threatening that they would be throwing a grenade. Identify yourself, they yelled. They knew I was somewhere in the dark. I tried not to move. They issued some military-style orders, "Left flank, right flank, turn left," they opened fire, rifle fire. I was keeping very silent and some two hours passed in this manner. They went away. I crossed the road and entered the woods above the road. I could not proceed towards the village because it was very steep. So I traversed the woods throughout the night, over some hills. It was very difficult to make progress. I was exhausted. And it was difficult to walk in the woods, through the thicket. At the crack of dawn I reached a mountain and a meadow. I managed to find some water, some unripe fruit, plums and apples, some wheat. I ate some wheat grains, managed to eat something, fell asleep. And this is how I managed to survive. After that night, I planned to cross a wood to enter a valley that day but I heard some noise, some trucks. It was a truck or a tractor, so it meant I couldn't proceed in that direction because there was somebody there and could be the site of a mass grave. So I hatched a plan to go in another direction. I reached a tarmacked road. I took that tarmacked road some 20, 30 metres to reach another wood, that was the second day. It was one and a half hours before sunset. I reached the tarmacked road, and I took the road towards the woods, some 20 metres, but when I took a look there, the road, the tarmac, was bloodstained, half a metre wide, a flow of blood in the direction of the commotion or noise. And as soon as I reached the woods where I was supposed to take a turn, a truck emerged right -- driving towards me. As soon as I took a look at the truck, I saw it was filled with dead bodies up to the height of the driver's cabin. And somebody shouted from the truck, "Look, there is the one who escaped yesterday." And the truck stopped, and it took about 30 or 40 metres for the truck to stop. The truck stopped, and since I heard what was said, I didn't dare go into the woods. I just continued walking along the road. I reached a bridge. The bridge is about ten metres wide and 15 metres long. There is no water beneath it. There is no woods there. It's an irrigation ditch or something. I crossed the bridge, I didn't turn around any more. I walked for a while, and then I looked back. It was going behind me. It reached the bridge, and was standing there and looking at me. I wasn't running or fleeing. I was just walking straight down along the street, and he kept looking at me. He thought I was a Serb, I guess, and at that point, the person turned back and started running back towards the truck. I turned into the ditch so if that Serb was still looking at me I wanted him to see me, that I was not a Serb. I wanted him to see me because he wanted to get me, to throw me on the truck and kill me and put me in the mass grave. I wanted him to see that it was me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If we could go into private session now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: So sir, you were telling us about how you were in a bus. Where were you being taken to?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: We were brought to Karakaj and we were told to report to the command and we set off to do that and then someone else said, "Go back, go to the truck and you can go together with this guy." It was a two tonne truck covered with tarpaulin. I went to the truck and then I could see that inside there were some other people who had been caught in the woods. There were 27 of them all together. And the two of us also, 29. Then they shouted out that they should all be tied up. And I did not -- I was not tied up. I was given a water bottle and I was told that if anybody wanted to drink, I was supposed to give them water to drink. So I wasn't tied up, and all the others were tied up. We were under the tarpaulin. One of our people said, "It's a good thing that the Red Cross is here. They will be accompanying us." So that's how we set off and we were being escorted by the Red Cross. And we were going through Bijeljina and we reached Batkovic where we were put in a camp. We received pallets there where we would sleep. We were issued two blankets, one we could put on the pallet, the second one we used to cover ourselves. If you had something to put under your head, very well; if not, that was it. That day, we shaved, all of us shaved. We had baths. We had haircuts. The Red Cross was there and they registered us that day. This was the 26th of August, I remember very well, if you want to write that down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how long approximately were you at the camp?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The 26th, not August. It's July actually. It was the 26th when I got there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And how long were you there until? What was your last date there? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross was registering us. The last day was actually the 24th of December, shortly before new years. That was when the last exchange took place. I spent a full five months in that camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And sir, where did you go once you were released from the camp?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: We were exchanged. Serbs came from Tuzla and us Muslims were brought from Batkovic, so this was an exchange that took place on the 24th of December, shortly before the new year.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And where did you go from there, from the exchange point?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I went to my family. I had grandchildren, a daughter-in-law, a daughter, my wife. I went to Gracanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, if I may, I will just -- I'd like to take you back to the 13th of July. You were mentioning that on that day, there were separations taking place. Could you tell us about it in a little more detail? Who was separating whom and how?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: There were two barricades, and they were letting through about 150 to 200 people who were supposed to go on the buses. They were letting them through. There was another barricade about 15 meters further along down the road and there were soldiers there who were immediately separating the men from the women and the children. That day, I came out, it was Thursday, the 13th of July, and every day people were coming out. This didn't happen just on that day. It went on every day for as long as this was going on. People were leaving every day. And the separation was also something that was ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And who was controlling these separations at both the barricades?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Serb soldiers in multi-coloured uniforms. They were conducting these separations. That's what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One thing, I just want to make one thing clear for clarity's sake, when the witness says, multi-coloured uniforms, we are referring to camouflage uniforms. I mean, I just want to make sure that one is equivalent to the other. Because most of the time, in other testimonies and other trip transcripts we have camouflage --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There was one more thing that I heard from the witness and I don't see it in the transcript, and I believe that the witness said that the separation was going for five days. I believe that is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Hasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's correct, because so many people couldn't leave in one day. What I'm saying -- what I'm talking about is what I went through on Thursday. I'm talking about what happened on that day but the same thing was going on during the other days, and the others told about that, that there was the separation that was being done, and these men didn't come. That's what it looked like as I was leaving and it's possible that this was going on throughout that whole period. The people couldn't all leave in one day, 30.000 people or more. They couldn't leave in a day. That's 100 per cent for sure. So it means that it took five days for all of them to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Sir, who was with you? Was any of your family with you when you were making it through these barriers?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: My grandchildren and my daughter-in-law were with me. My wife had fainted and my daughter had taken her to get some medical assistance and I was with my daughter-in-law and my grandchildren. I had a large water bottle with me so -- a canister so that we would have children [as interpreted]. I was carrying water and my small grandchildren were walking in front of me. And I quickly gave the water canister to one of the grandchildren so that they could have water and I turned aside, and the four small grandchildren, together with my daughter-in-law, went off by themselves and I guess they were loaded on to the truck. It was very crowded and people were struggling and pushing in front of the trucks in order to get on to the trucks as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And, sir, when you were being separated, do you remember what the person separating you from your family looked like, what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: They were wearing the multi-coloured uniforms, the soldiers' uniforms that the Serbian soldiers were wearing, multi-coloured uniforms. They were soldiers. Five or six soldiers at the barricade, they were holding hands, and if they wanted to let somebody through, they would let them through, women and children to one side, and men to the other side. "Go, you have to go that way."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And sir, when you mentioned multi-coloured uniform, you are talking about camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms, but they didn't have any camouflage on their heads. But just from the head down, they were wearing the multi-coloured uniforms, the Serb multi-coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, if these soldiers had weapons on them?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, they had rifles slung over their shoulders. They were holding hands and at one place they would let through 150 people and then the next barricade would hold firm and would direct people to go in a direction and they would have their rifles slung over their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. One final question: Can you please try to describe for us the impact that your separation, detention and attempted execution had on you, your family, your life?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't feel good, no. The effect -- I look back and think back to what happened. There are many people who have been traumatised, they live with the trauma. Many people will bear consequences, and the children who survived that and who remember what happened. That's it. It's not good.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could ask the next witness is waiting at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think there is a point in keeping him here because we haven't started with one cross-examination and I don't, even though you took less than the anticipated time, I'm not that sure that we will be able to finish all the cross-examinations in one hour. So I think Mr. Ruez can leave. Also we have to hand down our decision before he starts giving evidence, which you can expect first thing tomorrow morning. Thank you. So let's do some homework before -- yes, I see Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I would just like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In the event we do not finish with this witness today, or that we finish just towards the end, I -- there is one issue I would like to raise with the Trial Chamber which needs to be raised before the next witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what I suggest we do is we start with the cross-examinations now. How much time do you require to raise there matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No more than five minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But how much would you expect the Prosecution then to be engaged in it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It is an issue on which we have a disagreement and it deals with the way we will proceed with exhibits. Of course, pending the decision of the Trial Chamber whether the next witness will proceed or not at all, but the way we'll proceed with exhibits I think in five minutes, we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll allow ten minute towards the end. So whoever is cross-examining the witness we'll need to stop ten minutes to one. Yes, Defence team for Mr. Popovic? Mr. Zivanovic -- Mr. Hasic, the gentleman standing at the moment is Mr. Zivanovic and he is lead counsel for accused Popovic. He will go first. He will be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Hasic. I would like to remind you, you remember that you gave a statement to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. That was in 1996, on the 25th of May 1996, to be more precise. In that statement, apart from other things, when describing the events at Potocari, you stated that the first night, night of between 11th and 12th of July, was tranquil?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Nobody bothered us. Only the shells struck the perimeter of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
