utterances.text: So they did not land at Potocari, they landed in the distance, somewhere in the distance, not the place where the refugees were housed?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Well, the refugees crowded a place and the shells struck outside that area. I did not say that, so they struck the area around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is not what I meant to say. I meant to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I hate to interrupt you but I think we need to slow down, both of you, all right? Mr. Hasic, when Mr. Zivanovic has finished putting the question to you, we need you to pause a little bit before you answer it. The reason is we don't understand your language and it has to be translated to us. So we need that small interval --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody is interpreting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And that's why we need that pause of time so that the interpreters finish their interpretation to us and then you can proceed, all right? So allow five seconds before you start answering any question that -- and the same applies to you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the same applies to you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I won't count the seconds. I can give them some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So we can conclude that that night, between 11th and 12th of July, the UN facility at Potocari housing the refugees was not targeted by shells?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Shells landed around, as I told you. At that night when we arrived there, when the people gathered, shells did land around the facility, around the people, around all the buildings, not just one building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Mr. Meek for accused Beara will now be cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hasic, how are you?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'd like to thank you for coming here to testify and I just have a few matters I would like to clarify with you, if I could. The Prosecutor asked you, sir, if you could estimate the number of Muslim men being held with you at the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say. I know that they asked me but I cannot tell you, I know how many people in this -- in my room let alone in the whole school, because I could not get outside my room. They would rifle-butt me and it was impossible to walk around because we were not free to move. We would be risking our heads, our lives. Nobody asked us whether we were guilty of anything or something. Nobody interrogated us, interviewed us. They -- all they know was that we were of a different faith, that we were Muslims, and this is why we treated us so. This is how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, could you please estimate for me or tell me how many Muslim men were in your room, then, at the school?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: That room, they crammed so many people, as I've said, maybe 150 to 200 people. It was so crammed that if you stood up, there would be no place for you to sit down. You could not move around, even move your legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You also mentioned that throughout the day, at the school, they were continually killing people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: They did kill people. They would lead them away, outside. What I saw was that they beat one person, he was bloodstained. They would take people away. There were screams and moans outside and we could hear bursts of gunfire. We were not supposed to look out the window because we could be then hit by a burst of gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But you testified that the Serb soldiers were taking the men out continually, all day long; is that correct, from not only your room but from other rooms? Was that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did say from other rooms as well, they would take out people and kill them, not only from my room. I did not see them taking out people from other rooms but I saw what they did in my room but what happened in my room happened in other rooms so they were not spared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How many other rooms were there, if you know?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I never entered that school in peacetime. I did in wartime. I never had visited that school. I had not lived there. So I don't know it in great detail. There were class rooms and whatever is needed for a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then estimate approximately how many people were taken out of these various rooms and killed while you were there, sir?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I can tell you from my room, some seven people, from my room. From other rooms, I don't know how many were led away. I couldn't see. But there were moans and screams outside that could be heard, and they were constant, day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, you later were taken to another school in Pilica, correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Pilica, from Bratunac to Pilica, I was housed in that school and I was taken from Pilica to execution by firing squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasic, you testified about the Pilica school and you said that in the room where you were being kept, there were some children, 15 or 16 years of age. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, in my room, I know this very well, some 12 of them. They were lined up, they were looked at, and they said about them, "Avdic seeks people like this, maybe to be soldiers," I don't know. They were led away. How many of such people were in other rooms, maybe 100, 120, and I don't know what happened to them. I can't say whether they were murdered or they were taken to this place or to other place. What counts is that they are no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, frankly, sir, you don't know what happened to them. They could be alive and well and living in France today, correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe if they are alive they would have made contact, maybe some of them would survive and would come out to testify that they were at Pilica at that camp but nobody is around to testify that they survived that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasic?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I cannot say that they were murdered because I did not see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, sir, how you estimate that there were perhaps 100 to 120 children of this age range in the other rooms at the school, if you did not see them?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I did not see that, but I think that if there were 12 of them in my room, I'm not sure how many rooms there were, but if a dozen emerged from each of those rooms, this is my reckoning, approximate reckoning, that that would make up this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasic. I understand that answer, but you still cannot tell me how you even come up with the estimate of how many rooms were in the building, do you?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I did not make an estimate, but since we had large class rooms, maybe 10 class rooms were in the building and other rooms. I cannot tell you precisely how many. What I know precisely is that there were 12 children in my room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, was -- it was at Pilica that you learned of people being registered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Not at Pilica, while I was at Potocari I heard that some people were being registered at Potocari, where UNPROFOR or their headquarters was located, that people are being registered. I know of some who were registered but never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, I was looking at your testimony on page 33 of today's transcript, where the Madam Prosecutor asked you, "Did you see people being registered anywhere from Bratunac to your arrival in Pilica?" And your answer was: "I did not see that. I believe that they did the registration at the headquarters somewhere, where the Dutch government or defence was located." So is it your testimony now that this was not in Pilica, nor was it in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would leave it at that, Mr. Meek, because I don't think anyone doubts where.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. No one doubts where the Dutch government as it is in the transcript or defence was located. Everyone knows where they were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hasic, you've also testified that there were some Muslim men that were being interrogated. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: What I saw was that two people were taken out, interrogated, asked questions, and they were brought back. But I didn't see other people being brought back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Soljan, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: If Mr. Meek could just provides a reference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think you have any further questions on this, have you, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Not really on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have you need to be specific, as Ms. Soljan has pointed out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Page 32, line 20 and 21, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hasic, how long did the -- did the individuals -- how long were they interrogated or questioned?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Well, they were taken out, I don't know. They asked a couple of questions. Not long. And they were brought back to that place. I knew those two. They did not come back. They were later captured, taken away and killed because they did not cross over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you believe that there were other Muslim men from other rooms in the school being taken out and questioned also?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, in looking at your testimony today, it appears that at the first school you went to, you believe that you stayed there one night or perhaps two nights. Correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Correct, Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then at the second school, in Pilica, you stayed there either one night, perhaps two nights, you're not sure, correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Possibly two nights. On the 17th, the execution took place, 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, you went to Bratunac on the 12th, correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Can't be the 12th. It is -- it was the 13th, and I said it but you didn't write it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: 13th, and you stayed --

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: On the 14th and 15th, I was in Bratunac. Then we were dragged over to Pilica, so around the 17th it was the mass execution that took place, without any questions being asked whether we were guilty or not. Nobody was asked anything. Their aim was for you to cease existing. See, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But you just answered that you could have stayed one night in Bratunac and not two. And now you say it was two. I'm just asking you which was it? Was it one, was it two, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Maybe one, maybe two. It's possible two nights. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12 years have passed. It didn't happen yesterday. Somethings have, you know, lapsed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek. Thank you, Mr. Hasic. Now, Defence for Mr. Nikolic headed by Ms. Nikolic will go next. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hasic.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple of questions if you can assist me to understand some events that took place during the period that you described.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Today, you told us about several officers that you saw in Pilica who were standing in the shade and talking.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if those officers had automatic rifles with them?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I know very well. I remember well, it was hot, they were wearing light clothes. Their shirts were unbuttoned and they had an automatic rifle on their shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you were at the house, at the beginning of all of these ugly events?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You were told all of those who were detained would be investigated and after that you would be taken to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, they said, yes, would be a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you assumed you would be exchanged until you arrived at Pilica?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm going to go back with a few questions to the most serious part of the events that you went through. And those are the events on -- in the field near Pilica.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said today that according to your estimate, there were about 1.000 to 1500 bodies in that field.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: That was my estimate, an approximate estimate, but it was for sure between 1.000 and 1500 bodies. This is definitely 100 per cent for sure. I didn't give you a definite figure. It was an approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. For you it was a very difficult day, which has marked you for the rest of your life and I'm sure you were very frightened and you wanted to leave that place as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. All I could see was the backhoe loader trying to collect all the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There were many such bodies in the field. You saw a lot of bodies in the field; is that correct, but you could not count them?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No. I couldn't count them but there were a thousand, between a thousand to 1500, and that is where they found both of my brothers, who were older than me. One of them was five years older than me. The other one was seven years older than me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasic. I'd like to ask you a few questions about the exchange from Batkovic, when you were released in late December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I have a document here from the Srebrenica collection, which is from the republican commission for Srebrenica, and there are names mentioned in the document, I think that perhaps we could move into closed session so that I could put these questions to the witness so that we would not reveal the identity of some people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Nikolic. That's exactly what we will do. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Now, Defence team for Mr. Borovcanin, and Mr. Stojanovic will be going next. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ahmo, I'm going to ask you some questions relating to those first things that happened. Let's try to go in sequence, Tuesday, 11th of July, you said you came to Potocari; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the day that Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What time was it?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: When I came, perhaps it was around noon or maybe 2.00 p.m., something like that. I cannot really say exactly what time it was. Perhaps I didn't even have a watch at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were people already inside the factories?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you couldn't get inside?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't. I was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we are familiar with the layout, can you please tell us whether you're talking about one building or several buildings where the people were?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The people were in a number of buildings. I don't know exactly how many but perhaps there were five or six of these buildings, factories, that are there. There is the lead factory, the Zinc Factory, accumulator, Feros, perhaps some other ones. There were some other factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far are the buildings, how much apart are the buildings? How much of an area do they occupy?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: They are perhaps 60 metres apart, one factory from another. That was the distance between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be right if I said that the factories took up an area of a surface of 300 square metres where these buildings were?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No. It had to be more. You couldn't put them all in an area of 300 metres, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please try to tell us a little more precisely how far the buildings were apart from each other, these buildings where the people of Srebrenica were being placed?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The people were being placed in these buildings, in the factories. They are quite close to each other. Some are above the road, some are below the road. Maybe they are 50 to 60 metres apart, up to 100 metres, depending on the factory. And then there were people again in between the factories, because you couldn't fit 30.000 people into the buildings, all of them. That's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you really couldn't see all of the factories and know where all the people were, from the place where you were standing?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see everything. This is quite a large compound. I walked around a little bit, I would be bringing water to the children, going looking for water, so I was passing amongst the people. So I know that there were people all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would like to clarify something now, something that wasn't clear to me. You said today that you did not enter any of the factories but that you were outside.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That night, I stayed by myself. I had lost my family. They were somewhere amongst the people. And afterwards, when it got light, I walked around and I found my family. They were in the factory. The second night, all of us slept outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. I would like us to proceed in order. On the 11th, in the afternoon, and that night, you are in Potocari, the night of the 11th and the 12th you were separated from your family and you were sleeping outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, those two nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The night of the 11th to the 12th, the first night, you slept separately from your family?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was separated from my family. The second night I was together with my family outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So the second night, the night of the 12th to the 13th, you were with your family but you were not sleeping inside any of the factories?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No. On the 13th I left Potocari and went to Bratunac. Finally I hope it's clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that that first night, the night of the 11th to the 12th --

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not see that there were any killing or separation of people that night; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No. There was none of that the first night but it did happen on the second night. It was a catastrophe on the second night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly what I wanted to ask you.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about that catastrophe you're talking about the night from the 12th to the 13th, that was the second night that you spent there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The night of the 12th and the 13th, actually, I know that as the second night. That's what I'm talking about, the 12th to the 13th. In any case, it's the second night, on Tuesday, the 11th, I know very well was when Srebrenica fell. That's when we went down to Potocari. That's the first night. The second night was dangerous for many. Many lost their lives. Many were moaning that night, and the next day after that, on Thursday, Bratunac, Vuk Karadzic, where what food we had left was taken away from us so we would have nothing to eat. Yes, that's how it was. So that we would die of hunger, that we would be feeble, we would have no strength, that we would have nothing. They had the weapons. Our arms were tied.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about Bratunac now?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Bratunac and wherever you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like us to proceed step by step. It would be easier that way. We are going to stop now because we are going to talk about Potocari now. Those people whose moans and screams you heard on the second night in Potocari, did you see where they were being taken out from? Were they taken from inside the factory or were they taken away from the outside?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see that. I was outside. They were not taking them close by from me, perhaps they were taking away somebody from half a kilometre away and then from some other side completely. But you could hear them. Everybody would jump up around them and they would be saying things and then after that, you could hear the screaming and the moaning of those people who were being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see that, you just heard it?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just heard that. I trust what I see with my own eyes and what I hear with my own ears. I trust myself. And nobody can tell me that this wasn't so, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And all of this happened on the second night?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The second night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I would like to ask you to help us with this: Where did they take you? Which house? Where is that house in Potocari where you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: On the way out, away from the factories, as you pass the factories there was a house to the left side. That's the house where they took us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the direction of which, in the direction of Srebrenica or in the direction of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the direction of Bratunac, where we were going. It couldn't have been in the direction of Srebrenica because that's where I came from. Now I was going the other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So to a house on the left side, going in the direction of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the left side, in the direction of Bratunac, passed the factories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far is it from the main asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's about 15 to 20 metres off from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that a house with one floor or two floors, with an attic? Was it just a single-storey building?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The house had a ground floor and first floor. I don't know if it also had an attic. I wasn't really observing everything and seeing exactly how it looked, and I didn't have a pencil with me to be writing down all the dates and all that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ahmo, can you help us? Can you remember whether there were any tape, was there any tapes around the UN compound, the check-point?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I don't know about -- around the check-point, I'm sure that there were, I didn't see any but I'm sure that there were because wherever they did have a check-point, they had some tape or wire around the check-points. There were also sandbags on the -- on the ground. That's how they fortified them. They used sandbags to build up the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And were the people separated by tape, the place where they were, was nylon tape separating the people?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: No. That wasn't there. Then you would have needed to tape off the entire area of Potocari, but that wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who told you that? Where did you see that?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So are you telling us that there were no tapes or that you didn't see this tape?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it. Maybe there was some tape somewhere but not around the entire compound. I don't think so. In any case, I didn't see any. This was a large area that these people were occupying, the people were sitting, lying down, it was a large area. I didn't go around the edges of the area to check if there was any tape there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, on the 13th of July, the second day in Potocari, you were outside together with your family, is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: That night, that was the last night at Potocari, on the 13th, I was taken to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because of the following: When did they give out the bread and when you could give that bread to your grandchildren?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: It was the first night, from the 11th to the 12th, we arrived. And on the 12th they gave us bread. And I was out of there on the 13th. It was Thursday, the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we will be stopping in five minutes' time but before we do that, what are you trying to achieve? Are you attacking the credibility of the witness or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I want, through the testimony of this witness, I'm trying to position where the unit under the control of Mr. Borovcanin was, according to the indictment, because later on it will be made clear when they came to Potocari, whether they were there from the 11th to the 12th of July, and I'm going to agree with what the witness is saying and it is not my intention to compromise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest you go straight to that point because we have been going around and around in circles and I think what you've just said is more important to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Ahmo, what I'd like to ask you now is this: The two check-points that you mentioned, do you remember them, at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I can understand the objection. Yes, Ms. Soljan?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOLJAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, Your Honours, but his first name is Ahmo. He has a last name and I believe it would be appropriate to address him with respect and address him by his last name. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe it's the practice over there but I would tend to agree with you. If you could address him as Mr. Hasic I think it would be better. I mean -- it could lead to incidents. It has led to incidents in other cases, Mr. Stojanovic. In fact, I didn't like it in the beginning when you first started that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will address you as Mr. Hasic.

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Whichever way you want. You can call me a bucket. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, my question pertained to the two check-points that you mentioned. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: The two check-points of UNPROFOR at Potocari, I know that there was one, I don't know anything about two check-points. I never testified to that. There was the check-point of UNPROFOR where they had their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On your way to the buses, how was your progress to the buses organised?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Well, my movement was that I could move through the throng. I used to fetch water for my family. I could walk. But when -- as we proceeded towards the exit, it was terrible. Everybody was pushing and shoving others. Nobody could be stopped. People were shoving and pushing. But I would have progressed more slowly but I could not, because I was carried by the people and this is how we reached the exit point. There was the check-point, as I said, they would let a certain number of people through, 150, 200, as I testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question pertains to that check-point. As you said, barricade or point, where they would let through 150 to 200 people. Would -- were they letting through both men, women and children?

utterances.speaker: AHMO HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of them but the second check-point, some 15 metres away, was the place where they separated men from children and women. They would point men to go in the direction of the house, and women and children in the direction of buses or trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Here, if you -- the rest that is the three remaining Defence teams, if you could give me an indication of how much time you would require, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, between 30 and 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Haynes or Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I reckon Mr. Ruez needs to be here right after the first break tomorrow or rather to play it safe maybe he should be here right from the beginning. Mr. Usher you can accompany the witness out. Mr. Hasic, we will have to stop here and you come back tomorrow. You will be finished tomorrow morning or during the day any way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can take a break. It's only one day. I need to take a break, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The staff will make the arrangements for you that suit you most. Mr. Hasic, you are not to communicate -- one moment, let me finish. You're not to communicate with anyone between today and tomorrow on the subject matter of the events you are testifying upon or the subject matter of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see you tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, try to keep it short, please. Yes, Mr. Bourgon, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought there were no problems with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At there point in time, Mr. President, we are awaiting for, of course, a decision from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to hand a motion down as soon as you finish. If you want to hear it before we can proceed with it straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I anticipate that the witness will be proceeding because you just mentioned a few minutes ago that the witness will be proceeding tomorrow. So with this in mind, Mr. President I would like to address one issue which might bring some difficulties during the testimony of this witness. On 21 August, further to the order issued by the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution filed a submission in which it included a list of exhibits it intends to use with the first witnesses. Now, that includes witness number 1, witness Ruez. On this list, contained about 100 exhibits along with Rule 65 ter number, and in some cases ERN number, and in some cases references to exhibit number in past cases. Now, this allowed us to do the groundwork and to prepare for this witness and we located almost all of these 100 exhibits other than for maybe five to ten. The difficulty arose on the 24th of August, when we received a CD-ROM by the Prosecution and on this CD-ROM is -- you find about 260 pictures or exhibits intended to be used with Witness number 1, and on this CD-ROM, there are no longer any ERN numbers, no longer any 65 ter number. So it is not possible for us to make a match as to what the Prosecution wants to use with the list that was initially given to us or with the official list of the Prosecution dating back to 28 April. Moreover, on this CD-ROM, all over the exhibits, there are markings which have been added on the exhibits. Now, this was further complicated on 30th August whether we received an additional CD-ROM with about something like 14 additional pictures and some videos. I'll try to make this short. We are not worried with the markings that were added. We have been informed by -- my colleague has informed us that in order to save time, he would ask the witness to mark -- make markings in advance and if we can save time the Defence is always willing to assist the Court in saving sometime. So that's not our main problem. However, it is our understanding that if the Prosecution wants to use any exhibits, it must be an exhibit which was on its list, on this Rule 65 list dating back to 28 April. Now that's the object and purpose of Rule 65 ter is that -- to allow the Defence to prepare a case knowing which exhibits will be used. That's why, when the Prosecution wants to add new exhibits, it files a motion, like the latest motion was filed to try and add 300 new exhibits. Now, in this case, we have a witness that will appear tomorrow and we have some 280 exhibits and there is no way for us to tell whether these exhibits are or are not either on the e-court list or the Rule 65 list or any other list. I introduced this issue to my colleague last week - maybe we did not understand each other correctly - and we further spoke this morning. There is a misunderstanding, of course, as to what is the object and purpose of the Rule 65 ter. We believe that it must be there right now we can mot proceed without having references to that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Point taken. Mr. McCloskey would you like to address it now or tomorrow in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I should address it now, Your Honour. Mr. Ruez, the list that we originally gave them was basically the material used in the Krstic and the Blagojevic, including many video tapes. Mr. Ruez came back from France and gave us a revised list based on that material on a nice CD that had everything on it that we provided the Defence with and I haven't heard any objection on any photo or anything on that list. Defence is correct in that that CD doesn't have, we didn't go through the effort to try to figure out all the -- what 65 ter numbers went with the new CD but I can tell you, after he told me this issue I went with some of our legal help through all the new photos and most of them are repeats of the photos that have 65 ters. Some are stills from the videos that also had 65 ters. Others are a slightly better picture from a better angle or a better quality picture because many of our old exhibits weren't the best quality, frankly and we now had access to a better digital. So I went through each of the -- some 24 crime areas and did not find any surprises, any new pictures, that were -- would have surprised the accused in any way. There are for example, Cerska valley, he's put more Cerska valley pictures, there are more holes in the ground that they dug than were on the 65 ter list but fundamentally I didn't see any surprises. The one thing a couple of pictures were the hills where the column was leaving from which was an issue that had been brought up that I thought and Mr. Ruez thought you may be interested in. There are some pictures of those hills but not just like the ones he's provided. But otherwise I didn't see any surprise. No one's told me of any surprise and if there is some surprise I will consider withdrawing the picture if it's a big deal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I suggest that you continue to try and iron this out between you, between now and tomorrow. I don't anticipate a great problem as we go along, if you identify any of these and if they require a decision to be taken it will be taken. In the meantime let's proceed with anticipated oral version of the decision on the Ruez testimony that I will sign -- I have already signed, will be filed later on. Basically -- yes, are you still standing, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I'd like to reply briefly because there is new material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When the problems arise, we will take them in their stride and we will decide accordingly. I have taken the point and then I've heard what Mr. McCloskey had to say as well. I still don't think there will be major problems and, if a problem arises, we will tackle it there and then. So the position is as follows in relation to the Defence motion, joint motion, requesting the termination as to the admissibility of testimony of Jean-Rene Ruez. I've taken note of all the filings and all the submissions. We considered that the Prosecution, first of all we have taken note that both of you declared that you agree and accept the relevant jurisprudence of the -- of the Tribunal. We also take note of the Prosecution's assurance to the Defence, Trial Chamber, that they will neither -- was neither going to ask Mr. Ruez to speculate or make an appropriate conclusion that will not be helpful to the Court to get into the problems, et cetera. That we've also considered that although the transcripts of the evidence given by the witness in previous cases do indeed raise concern regarding the scope and form of his testimony, the Trial Chamber is of the view that there is no need for pre-emptive ruling on the contents of his evidence in the current case. Then ultimately and this is the cornerstone of the decision that we have the overall responsibility under our rules of overseeing the proceedings of trial in light of the principles laid down both in the Statute and our Rules, particularly as described in Rule 90, to wit exercise control over the mode and order of interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to, first, make the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth, and, second, to avoid needless consumption of time. We do also make a point in our decision that we would have preferred that from -- the Prosecution to have provided the Defence with an early witness statement. That would have facilitated much and probably avoided all this incident. And precisely because of this concern that we have, we do enjoin you to fully explain to the witness, either during the remaining briefing period, if there is any left, or before he is called to give evidence, the substantives of this decision, which we will be handing down. The rest I think you can safely leave in our hands and we'll take good care of it. Thank you. We will resume tomorrow morning. I would take it that the first session will be still with this witness. Thank you.
